u:webdev-web-0-client-server-model.title: Client–server model
u:webdev-web-0-client-server-model.summary: The browser (client) requests resources; a server responds. The web is a request/response conversation over HTTP.

blocks.text: A **client** (browser, mobile app) sends a request to a **server**, which processes it and returns a response. The client drives; the server never pushes unsolicited data over plain HTTP (that needs WebSockets/SSE).
Stateless by default: each HTTP request is independent — the server doesn't remember the last one. State is re-created with cookies, tokens, or sessions.

mcqs.q: In the client–server model, who initiates a plain HTTP exchange?
mcqs.explain: The client sends the request; the server responds.
Each request is independent; state is layered on with cookies/tokens.

mcqs.q: To let a server push data to the client in real time you'd use:
mcqs.explain: Plain HTTP is client-initiated; WebSockets/Server-Sent Events enable server push.

u:webdev-web-1-dns-resolution.title: DNS resolution
u:webdev-web-1-dns-resolution.summary: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address before the browser can connect.

blocks.text: Before a request can be sent, the domain (e.g. `example.com`) must be resolved to an **IP address**. The browser checks its cache, then the OS, then a **recursive resolver**, which walks root → TLD → authoritative name servers.
Results are cached with a **TTL**. A low TTL means faster propagation of changes but more lookups; a high TTL means fewer lookups but slower updates.

options: A domain name to an IP address
mcqs.explain: DNS maps human-readable names to IP addresses.

options: How long the result is cached
mcqs.explain: TTL is the cache lifetime of the record.

mcqs.q: The resolver that walks root → TLD → authoritative servers is the:
mcqs.explain: A recursive resolver performs the full lookup on the client's behalf.

u:webdev-web-2-http-request-response-lif.title: HTTP request/response lifecycle
u:webdev-web-2-http-request-response-lif.summary: A request has a method, URL, headers and optional body; the response has a status, headers and body.

blocks.text: A request carries a **method** (GET/POST/…), a **path**, **headers**, and an optional **body**. The response carries a **status code**, **headers**, and a **body**. TCP (and TLS for HTTPS) is established first; HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection.
GET should have no body and be safe/idempotent; POST sends a body and creates/changes state.

mcqs.q: Which part is common to BOTH request and response?
mcqs.explain: Both requests and responses carry headers; status is response-only, method is request-only.

options: Has no body and is safe
mcqs.explain: GET is safe/idempotent and normally bodiless; GETs are cacheable.

mcqs.q: HTTPS adds which layer before HTTP?
mcqs.explain: HTTPS runs HTTP over a TLS-encrypted connection.

u:webdev-web-3-status-codes-worth-knowin.title: Status codes worth knowing cold
u:webdev-web-3-status-codes-worth-knowin.summary: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

blocks.text: 401 vs 403: 401 means 'who are you?' (authenticate); 403 means 'I know you, but no' (not authorized).

mcqs.q: Which status means the request was understood but the user isn't authenticated?
mcqs.explain: 401 Unauthorized = authentication required/failed.
201 Created signals a new resource was made.
5xx codes are server errors; 4xx are client errors.

u:webdev-web-4-headers-content-type-cach.title: Headers: content-type, cache-control, auth
u:webdev-web-4-headers-content-type-cach.summary: Headers carry metadata: what the body is, how to cache it, and who's calling.

items: **Content-Type** tells the receiver how to parse the body (e.g. `application/json`).
**Cache-Control** governs caching (`no-store`, `max-age=3600`, `public/private`).
**Authorization** carries credentials (e.g. `Bearer <token>`).

blocks.text: A wrong Content-Type is a classic bug: sending JSON as `text/plain` makes many servers skip body parsing.

mcqs.q: Which header tells the server the body is JSON?
mcqs.explain: Content-Type declares the body's media type.
no-store forbids storing the response anywhere.

mcqs.q: A bearer token is usually sent in the:
mcqs.explain: Authorization: Bearer <token> is the standard.

u:webdev-web-5-cors-what-actually-trigge.title: CORS — what actually triggers preflight
u:webdev-web-5-cors-what-actually-trigge.summary: CORS is a browser rule; non-simple cross-origin requests send an OPTIONS preflight first.

blocks.text: **CORS** lets a server opt in to being called from other origins. The browser (not the server) enforces it. **Simple** requests (GET/POST with simple headers) go straight through; anything else (custom headers, PUT/DELETE, JSON content-type with certain conditions) triggers a **preflight `OPTIONS`** request the server must answer with the right `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers.
CORS errors are browser-side. The request often still reaches the server; the browser just blocks the JS from reading the response. curl/Postman won't show a CORS error.

mcqs.explain: The browser enforces the same-origin policy and CORS relaxations.

mcqs.q: A preflight request uses which method?
mcqs.explain: The browser sends an OPTIONS preflight for non-simple requests.

mcqs.q: Why might a CORS error not appear in curl?
options: curl isn't a browser and doesn't enforce CORS
mcqs.explain: CORS is a browser policy; non-browser clients ignore it.

u:webdev-web-6-cookies-vs-localstorage-v.title: Cookies vs localStorage vs sessionStorage
u:webdev-web-6-cookies-vs-localstorage-v.summary: Cookies auto-send to the server; localStorage/sessionStorage are client-only key/value stores.

blocks.text: Auth tokens in cookies (esp. HttpOnly) resist XSS reads; tokens in localStorage are readable by any script (XSS risk) but immune to CSRF.

mcqs.q: Which store is automatically attached to HTTP requests?
mcqs.explain: Cookies are sent with matching requests automatically.
sessionStorage lives only for the tab's session.

mcqs.q: An HttpOnly cookie is NOT readable by:
mcqs.explain: HttpOnly blocks JS access, mitigating token theft via XSS.

u:webdev-web-7-browser-rendering-parse-c.title: Browser rendering: parse, CSSOM, layout, paint
u:webdev-web-7-browser-rendering-parse-c.summary: HTML→DOM, CSS→CSSOM, combine into the render tree, then layout (geometry) and paint (pixels).

items: Parse HTML into the **DOM** tree.
Parse CSS into the **CSSOM**.
Combine into the **render tree** (visible nodes + styles).
**Layout/reflow**: compute each box's size and position.
**Paint**: fill in pixels; **composite** layers to the screen.

blocks.text: Changing geometry (width, top) triggers layout; changing only paint properties (color) skips it; `transform`/`opacity` can be composited on the GPU — cheapest to animate.

mcqs.q: The DOM is built by parsing:
mcqs.explain: HTML parses into the DOM; CSS parses into the CSSOM.
Layout/reflow computes geometry.

mcqs.q: Cheapest properties to animate smoothly are usually:
mcqs.explain: transform/opacity can be GPU-composited without layout/paint.

u:webdev-web-8-critical-rendering-path.title: Critical rendering path
u:webdev-web-8-critical-rendering-path.summary: The steps from bytes to first pixels; minimizing render-blocking resources speeds first paint.

blocks.text: The **critical rendering path** is everything the browser must do to turn HTML/CSS/JS into pixels. CSS is **render-blocking**; synchronous `<script>` is **parser-blocking**. Reducing and deferring these speeds up first paint.
Put CSS in the head, load JS with `defer`/`async`, and inline critical CSS to shorten the path.

mcqs.q: Which resource is render-blocking by default?
mcqs.explain: The browser won't paint until required CSS is processed.

options: Runs it after HTML parsing, in order
mcqs.explain: defer waits until parsing completes and preserves order.

mcqs.q: Inlining critical CSS helps because it:
mcqs.explain: Critical CSS inline avoids a blocking stylesheet fetch for first paint.

u:webdev-html-0-semantic-elements-and-wh.title: Semantic elements and why they matter
u:webdev-html-0-semantic-elements-and-wh.summary: Tags like header/nav/main/article describe meaning, aiding accessibility and SEO.

blocks.text: **Semantic** elements (`<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<section>`, `<footer>`) describe the role of content, not just its look. Screen readers and search engines rely on them; a page of `<div>`s conveys no structure.
Use one `<main>` per page and headings in order (h1→h2→h3) — assistive tech builds a document outline from them.

mcqs.explain: Semantics give meaning that AT and crawlers use.

mcqs.q: How many <main> elements should a page have?
mcqs.explain: A page should have a single <main> landmark.
<article> conveys meaning; div/span are generic.

u:webdev-html-1-forms-and-validation.title: Forms and validation
u:webdev-html-1-forms-and-validation.summary: Native inputs, required/type/pattern attributes, and the constraint validation API.

blocks.text: HTML forms support **native validation** via attributes: `required`, `type="email"`, `min`/`max`, `pattern`. The browser blocks submission and shows messages. JavaScript's **Constraint Validation API** (`checkValidity()`, `setCustomValidity()`) customizes it.
Client validation is UX, not security — always re-validate on the server. A malicious client can bypass the browser entirely.

mcqs.q: Native form validation should be treated as:
options: UX only — re-validate on the server
mcqs.explain: Client validation improves UX but can be bypassed; the server must validate.

mcqs.q: Which attribute makes a field mandatory?
mcqs.explain: The `required` attribute enforces presence.
The email input type validates the address format.

u:webdev-html-2-accessibility-labels-rol.title: Accessibility: labels, roles, alt, focus order
u:webdev-html-2-accessibility-labels-rol.summary: Every control needs a name; images need alt; focus order must be logical.

items: Associate a **`<label for>`** with every input so it has an accessible name.
Give informative images **`alt`** text; decorative images `alt=""`.
Use native elements first; add ARIA **roles** only when no native element fits.
Keep a logical **tab order** and visible focus outlines.

blocks.text: The first rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if a native HTML element already does the job.

mcqs.explain: Empty alt tells screen readers to skip decorative images.

mcqs.q: The best accessible name for an input comes from:
mcqs.explain: A <label for> provides a reliable accessible name; placeholders are not labels.

mcqs.q: The first rule of ARIA is:
mcqs.explain: Use ARIA only when a native element can't express the semantics.

u:webdev-html-3-meta-tags-and-seo-basics.title: Meta tags and SEO basics
u:webdev-html-3-meta-tags-and-seo-basics.summary: title, meta description, viewport, and Open Graph tags shape search and sharing.

items: `<title>` and `<meta name="description">` drive the search snippet.
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` enables responsive mobile layout.
Open Graph tags (`og:title`, `og:image`) control link previews on social platforms.

blocks.text: One `<h1>`, descriptive titles, clean URLs, and fast load all help SEO more than meta-keyword stuffing (ignored by Google).

mcqs.q: The viewport meta tag is needed for:
mcqs.explain: It tells mobile browsers to use the device width.
og:* tags shape how a shared link appears.

mcqs.q: Which is largely ignored by Google today?
mcqs.explain: The keywords meta tag is ignored; title/description still matter.

u:webdev-html-4-data-attributes.title: data-* attributes
u:webdev-html-4-data-attributes.summary: Custom data-* attributes store extra data on elements, read via dataset.

blocks.text: **`data-*`** attributes attach custom data to any element without breaking validation, e.g. `<li data-id="42">`. Read them in JS via `element.dataset.id`.
Great for hooking behavior/analytics to elements without polluting classes or ids.

mcqs.explain: dataset camelCases the suffix: data-user-id → dataset.userId.

options: Valid custom attributes for any element
mcqs.explain: They're standard, valid on any HTML element.

mcqs.q: A good use of data-* is:
mcqs.explain: Attach identifiers/metadata; keep styling in classes.

u:webdev-css-0-box-model-and-box-sizing.title: Box model and box-sizing
u:webdev-css-0-box-model-and-box-sizing.summary: Every element is a box: content + padding + border + margin. box-sizing changes what width means.

blocks.text: The box model layers **content → padding → border → margin**. By default `width` sets only the content box, so padding/border add to the rendered size. `box-sizing: border-box` makes `width` include padding and border — far more intuitive.
A common reset: `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` so widths behave predictably.

mcqs.explain: border-box counts padding and border inside the width.
Margin is the outermost layer, outside the border.
content-box is the CSS default.

u:webdev-css-1-specificity-and-the-casca.title: Specificity and the cascade
u:webdev-css-1-specificity-and-the-casca.summary: When rules conflict, specificity + source order decide; inline > id > class > element.

blocks.text: The **cascade** resolves conflicts using origin, **specificity**, then source order. Specificity is roughly (inline, ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements). A higher category always wins.
`!important` overrides normal specificity — avoid it; it starts specificity wars. Prefer a more specific selector or better structure.

mcqs.q: Which selector has the highest specificity?
mcqs.explain: IDs outrank classes, which outrank element selectors.

mcqs.q: When specificity ties, the winner is:
mcqs.explain: Equal specificity is broken by source order (last wins).
It breaks the natural cascade and is hard to override.

u:webdev-css-2-position-static-relative-.title: Position: static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky
u:webdev-css-2-position-static-relative-.summary: Positioning schemes control how an element is placed and what it's offset from.

rows: Default; in normal flow, offsets ignored
In flow, offset from its normal spot; creates a positioning context
Removed from flow; positioned to nearest positioned ancestor
Removed from flow; positioned to the viewport
Toggles between relative and fixed at a scroll threshold

blocks.text: `absolute` anchors to the nearest ancestor with `position` other than static — a common gotcha when it jumps to the body.

mcqs.explain: It anchors to the nearest ancestor with a non-static position.

mcqs.q: Which sticks to the viewport regardless of scroll?
mcqs.explain: fixed is anchored to the viewport.

options: relative until a threshold, then fixed
mcqs.explain: Sticky toggles to fixed once a scroll offset is reached.

u:webdev-css-3-flexbox.title: Flexbox
u:webdev-css-3-flexbox.summary: One-dimensional layout: distribute space along a main axis with justify/align.

blocks.text: **Flexbox** lays items along a **main axis** (row/column). `justify-content` distributes along the main axis; `align-items` aligns on the cross axis. `flex: 1` lets items grow to fill space.
`flex-direction` sets which axis is 'main'. Swapping it swaps what justify-content vs align-items control.

mcqs.explain: Flexbox handles a single axis (row or column).
justify-content works on the main axis; align-items on the cross axis.
flex-grow:1 shares leftover space equally.

u:webdev-css-4-grid.title: Grid
u:webdev-css-4-grid.summary: Two-dimensional layout: define rows and columns with fr, gaps, and areas.

blocks.text: **CSS Grid** lays out in two dimensions. `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)` makes three equal columns; `gap` adds spacing; named `grid-template-areas` map regions.
Use Grid for the page/section skeleton (rows AND columns); use Flexbox for a single row/column of items. They compose well.

mcqs.explain: fr distributes remaining space in fractions.
Grid handles rows and columns together.
It repeats a 1fr column three times.

u:webdev-css-5-responsive-design-and-med.title: Responsive design and media queries
u:webdev-css-5-responsive-design-and-med.summary: Adapt layout to screen size with fluid units and @media breakpoints; design mobile-first.

blocks.text: **Responsive** pages adapt to any screen using fluid units and **media queries**: `@media (min-width: 768px) { … }`. A **mobile-first** approach writes the base styles for small screens and layers enhancements upward with `min-width`.
Combine media queries with flexible layouts (Flex/Grid) and relative units — breakpoints alone aren't 'responsive'.

mcqs.q: Mobile-first CSS uses which query direction?
mcqs.explain: Mobile-first layers larger styles with min-width.
@media applies rules based on device/viewport features.
Fluid units and Flex/Grid adapt; fixed pixels don't.

u:webdev-css-6-units-rem-em-vh-vw-ch.title: Units: rem, em, vh, vw, %, ch
u:webdev-css-6-units-rem-em-vh-vw-ch.summary: Relative units scale with context; rem is root-relative, em is parent-relative.

blocks.text: Prefer `rem` for consistent, accessible sizing (respects the user's root font); `em` compounds and can surprise you when nested.

mcqs.explain: rem = root em, based on the html element's font-size.
vh is a percentage of the viewport's height.

mcqs.q: Why can nested `em` values surprise you?
mcqs.explain: em is relative to the current element, so nesting multiplies.

blocks.text: **Pseudo-classes** (`:hover`, `:focus`, `:nth-child`, `:disabled`) target an element in a particular **state**. **Pseudo-elements** (`::before`, `::after`, `::placeholder`) style a **part** of an element or inject generated content (with `content:`).
Single colon = pseudo-class (state); double colon = pseudo-element (a sub-part). `::before` needs a `content` property to render.

mcqs.explain: It matches an element in the focused state.
Generated content requires the content property.
:: marks pseudo-elements; : marks pseudo-classes.

u:webdev-css-8-transitions-and-animation.title: Transitions and animations
u:webdev-css-8-transitions-and-animation.summary: Transitions interpolate between two states; @keyframes animations define multi-step motion.

blocks.text: A **transition** smoothly interpolates a property when it changes (e.g. on `:hover`): `transition: transform .2s ease`. **Animations** use `@keyframes` for multi-step, looping, or autoplaying motion.
Animate `transform` and `opacity` for 60fps; animating `width`/`top` forces layout each frame and stutters.

mcqs.explain: Transitions run when a property changes between two values.
@keyframes define named multi-step animations.
transform/opacity avoid layout and can be GPU-composited.

u:webdev-css-9-z-index-and-stacking-cont.title: z-index and stacking contexts
u:webdev-css-9-z-index-and-stacking-cont.summary: z-index orders overlapping elements — but only within the same stacking context.

blocks.text: `z-index` controls paint order of **positioned** elements, but only **within a stacking context**. Properties like `position` + `z-index`, `opacity < 1`, `transform`, and `filter` create new stacking contexts — a child can never escape its parent's context.
A huge z-index that 'doesn't work' is usually trapped in a parent stacking context created by an ancestor's transform/opacity.

mcqs.q: z-index only applies to elements that are:
mcqs.explain: z-index needs a position other than static.

mcqs.q: Which creates a new stacking context?
mcqs.explain: opacity<1 (and transform/filter) establish a stacking context.

mcqs.q: A child element's z-index is compared:
mcqs.explain: Stacking is resolved per context; children can't outrank a sibling context.

u:webdev-js-0-var-let-const-and-tdz.title: var, let, const and TDZ
u:webdev-js-0-var-let-const-and-tdz.summary: let/const are block-scoped; accessing them before declaration is the temporal dead zone.

blocks.text: `var` is function-scoped and hoisted as `undefined`. `let`/`const` are **block-scoped** and live in the **temporal dead zone (TDZ)** from the start of the block until their declaration — accessing them there throws. `const` can't be reassigned (but objects it holds are still mutable).
Default to `const`; use `let` when you must reassign; avoid `var`.

mcqs.explain: let/const are in the TDZ until declared.

options: obj can't be reassigned, but its props can change
mcqs.explain: const binds the reference; the object stays mutable.
var is function-scoped, not block-scoped.

u:webdev-js-1-hoisting.title: Hoisting
u:webdev-js-1-hoisting.summary: Declarations are processed first; var/functions hoist, but initializations don't.

blocks.text: **Hoisting** moves declarations to the top of their scope at compile time. Function **declarations** are fully hoisted (callable before their line). `var` is hoisted but initialized to `undefined`. `let`/`const` are hoisted but not initialized (TDZ).
Function *expressions* assigned to `var`/`const` are NOT callable before the assignment line.

mcqs.q: A function declaration can be called:
mcqs.explain: Function declarations are fully hoisted.
var initializes to undefined when hoisted.
const function expressions are in the TDZ until assigned.

u:webdev-js-2-scope-and-lexical-scope.title: Scope and lexical scope
u:webdev-js-2-scope-and-lexical-scope.summary: Scope is where a variable is visible; lexical scope is determined by where code is written.

blocks.text: **Scope** determines variable visibility. JavaScript uses **lexical (static) scope**: an inner function can access variables from where it was **defined**, not where it's called. Nested functions form a scope chain resolved outward.
Lexical scope is the foundation of closures.

options: Lexical (based on where code is written)
mcqs.explain: JS resolves variables by their location in the source.

mcqs.q: An inner function can read variables from:
mcqs.explain: The scope chain reaches outward to enclosing scopes.
Closures rely on lexical scope capturing outer variables.

u:webdev-js-3-closures-and-a-real-use-ca.title: Closures — and a real use case
u:webdev-js-3-closures-and-a-real-use-ca.summary: A closure is a function bundled with the variables from where it was created.

blocks.text: A **closure** is formed when a function 'remembers' variables from its lexical scope even after that scope has returned. It's the basis for data privacy, factories, and stable callbacks.
Closures capture the variable, not a snapshot — a classic bug is a loop with `var` where every callback sees the final value (use `let`).

options: A copy of the caller's stack
mcqs.explain: It retains access to its lexical environment.
They encapsulate private variables.

mcqs.q: A loop capturing `var i` in callbacks tends to:
options: Show the final i in all callbacks
mcqs.explain: var is shared; use let to capture per-iteration values.

u:webdev-js-4-this-in-every-calling-cont.title: this in every calling context
u:webdev-js-4-this-in-every-calling-cont.summary: 'this' is set by how a function is called: method, plain call, new, or bound.

items: **Method call** `obj.fn()` → `this` is `obj`.
**Plain call** `fn()` → `this` is undefined (strict) or the global object.
**Constructor** `new Fn()` → `this` is the new instance.
**Arrow function** → no own `this`; it uses the enclosing lexical `this`.

blocks.text: Passing a method as a callback (`setTimeout(obj.fn)`) loses `this`. Bind it or wrap in an arrow.

mcqs.explain: A method call binds this to the object before the dot.
Arrows have no own this; they inherit it lexically.
Constructors bind this to the fresh instance.

u:webdev-js-5-call-apply-bind.title: call, apply, bind
u:webdev-js-5-call-apply-bind.summary: Explicitly set 'this': call/apply invoke now, bind returns a new bound function.

rows: Invoke now with args as an array
Return a new function permanently bound to thisArg

blocks.text: Remember: **A**pply = **A**rray. `bind` doesn't call — it returns a function to call later.

mcqs.q: Which returns a new function instead of calling immediately?
mcqs.explain: bind returns a bound copy; call/apply invoke right away.
apply passes arguments as an array.

mcqs.q: To fix a method losing `this` in a callback you can:
mcqs.explain: bind (or an arrow wrapper) preserves this.

u:webdev-js-6-arrow-functions-vs-regular.title: Arrow functions vs regular functions
u:webdev-js-6-arrow-functions-vs-regular.summary: Arrows have no own this/arguments and can't be constructors; concise for callbacks.

items: Arrows have **no own `this`** (lexical), no `arguments` object, and can't be used with `new`.
Regular functions get `this` from the call site and have `arguments`.
Use arrows for callbacks/closures; use regular functions for methods and constructors.

blocks.text: Don't use an arrow as an object method if you need `this` to be the object — it won't be.

mcqs.explain: Arrows lack their own this, arguments, and can't be new'd.

mcqs.q: For an object method needing `this` = the object, use:
mcqs.explain: Regular functions bind this to the calling object.
Their concise lexical-this form suits callbacks.

u:webdev-js-7-prototypes-and-the-prototy.title: Prototypes and the prototype chain
u:webdev-js-7-prototypes-and-the-prototy.summary: Objects delegate to their prototype; lookups walk the chain until found or null.

blocks.text: Every object has an internal link to a **prototype**. Property lookups that miss on the object walk up the **prototype chain** until found or reaching `null`. This is how methods are shared without copying them onto every instance.
`Array.prototype.map` lives once on the prototype; all arrays delegate to it via the chain.

mcqs.q: A missing property triggers a lookup:
mcqs.explain: Lookups delegate to the prototype chain.
The chain terminates at null (Object.prototype's prototype).

mcqs.q: Shared methods on a prototype mean:
options: One copy shared by all instances
mcqs.explain: Prototype methods avoid duplicating functions per instance.

u:webdev-js-8-classes-and-inheritance.title: Classes and inheritance
u:webdev-js-8-classes-and-inheritance.summary: class is syntax over prototypes; extends/super set up inheritance.

blocks.text: `class` is **syntactic sugar** over prototypes. `extends` sets up inheritance and `super()` calls the parent constructor. Methods defined in a class live on the prototype, so instances share them.
You must call `super(...)` before using `this` in a subclass constructor.

mcqs.explain: class is sugar over the prototype system.

mcqs.q: In a subclass constructor you must call super() before:
mcqs.explain: this is uninitialized until super() runs.
Methods live on the prototype and are shared.

u:webdev-js-9-vs-and-coercion-rules.title: == vs === and coercion rules
u:webdev-js-9-vs-and-coercion-rules.summary: === compares without type coercion; == coerces types first (avoid it).

blocks.text: `===` is **strict equality**: same type and value, no coercion. `==` is **loose equality**: it coerces operands to a common type first, producing surprising results (`0 == ''`, `null == undefined`).
Use `===` by default. The one common `==` exception: `x == null` checks for both null and undefined.

mcqs.explain: Strict equality skips type coercion.
Loose equality coerces both to 0, so it's true — a reason to avoid ==.

mcqs.q: `x == null` is a handy shorthand for:
mcqs.explain: == null matches both null and undefined.

u:webdev-js-10-shallow-vs-deep-copy.title: Shallow vs deep copy
u:webdev-js-10-shallow-vs-deep-copy.summary: Spread/Object.assign copy one level; nested objects stay shared without a deep clone.

blocks.text: A **shallow copy** (`{...obj}`, `Object.assign`, `slice`) duplicates the top level but nested objects are still **shared references**. A **deep copy** clones everything — via `structuredClone(obj)` (modern) or a recursive clone.
Mutating a nested object in a 'copy' also mutates the original if you only did a shallow copy.

mcqs.explain: Spread copies only the first level.
structuredClone deep-copies most values natively.

mcqs.q: After a shallow copy, editing a nested object:
mcqs.explain: Nested references are shared in a shallow copy.

u:webdev-js-11-pass-by-value-vs-referenc.title: Pass by value vs reference
u:webdev-js-11-pass-by-value-vs-referenc.summary: Primitives are passed by value; objects are passed by a copied reference.

u:webdev-jsasync-0-call-stack.summary: The stack tracks function calls; JS runs one thing at a time (single-threaded).

blocks.text: A **Promise** represents a value that may not be ready yet — it's `pending`, then `fulfilled` or `rejected`. `.then` handles fulfillment, `.catch` handles rejection, `.finally` runs either way. Chaining returns new promises.

u:webdev-jsasync-7-async-await-and-error.summary: async functions return promises; await pauses; wrap in try/catch for errors.

blocks.text: An `async` function always returns a **promise**. `await` pauses until a promise settles, letting you write async code that reads synchronously. Errors from awaited promises are caught with **try/catch**.

u:webdev-react-2-rendering-and-re-render.summary: A component re-renders when its state or props change (or its parent re-renders).

blocks.text: React re-runs a component's function to produce new virtual DOM when its **state** or **props** change, or when its **parent** re-renders. It then **diffs** against the previous tree and updates only what changed in the real DOM.

u:webdev-react-3-usestate-and-batching.summary: useState holds state; multiple updates in one event are batched into one render.

blocks.text: `express.json()` parses JSON request bodies into `req.body`; `express.urlencoded()` handles form posts. Always **validate** the parsed body (e.g. with Zod/Joi) before using it — never trust client input.
Skipping validation invites injection, type bugs, and crashes from unexpected shapes.

mcqs.explain: It parses the JSON body into req.body.

options: Before using it (never trust the client)
mcqs.explain: Server-side validation is mandatory.

mcqs.q: A schema library for validation is:
mcqs.explain: Zod/Joi validate and type request payloads.

u:webdev-node-7-environment-variables-an.title: Environment variables and config
u:webdev-node-7-environment-variables-an.summary: Keep secrets and per-environment config out of code, in env vars.

blocks.text: **Environment variables** (`process.env.X`) hold config and secrets that differ per environment (DB URL, API keys). Load them from a `.env` file in development (e.g. dotenv), but **never commit** it.
Hard-coding secrets in source (and pushing to Git) is a top security mistake — rotate any key that lands in a repo.

mcqs.q: Secrets like DB URLs belong in:
mcqs.explain: Config/secrets go in env vars, not code.
It holds secrets; keep it out of version control.

mcqs.q: You read env vars in Node via:
mcqs.explain: process.env exposes environment variables.

u:webdev-node-8-async-error-handling-pat.title: Async error handling patterns
u:webdev-node-8-async-error-handling-pat.summary: Await can reject; wrap handlers so errors reach Express instead of crashing.

blocks.text: An unhandled rejection in an async route won't be caught by Express automatically. Wrap async handlers in try/catch and call `next(err)`, or use a helper (`asyncHandler`) / `express-async-errors` so rejections flow to error middleware.

const asyncHandler = fn => (req, res, next) =>
  Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);

mcqs.q: An unhandled async rejection in a route:
options: Won't reach Express error middleware by default
mcqs.explain: You must forward it with next(err) or a wrapper.

options: Wrap handlers so rejections call next(err)
mcqs.explain: asyncHandler forwards rejections to error middleware.

options: Catching the promise and calling next
mcqs.explain: It .catch(next)s the handler's promise.

u:webdev-api-0-rest-principles.title: REST principles
u:webdev-api-0-rest-principles.summary: REST is stateless, resource-oriented, and uses HTTP methods uniformly.

blocks.text: **REST** models the API as **resources** addressed by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods, communicated **statelessly** (each request self-contained). Responses should be cacheable where sensible and use a uniform interface.
Statelessness means the server keeps no client session between requests — auth travels with each request (token/cookie).

mcqs.explain: REST is stateless and models resources.
Resources are the core abstraction.

options: Each request carries its own context
mcqs.explain: No server-side per-client state between requests.

u:webdev-api-1-resource-naming-conventio.title: Resource naming conventions
u:webdev-api-1-resource-naming-conventio.summary: Use plural nouns and hierarchy; let HTTP methods express the verb.

items: Use **plural nouns**: `/users`, `/users/42/orders`.
Avoid verbs in paths — the **method** is the verb (`GET /users`, not `/getUsers`).
Nest to show relationships: `/users/42/posts`.

blocks.text: Keep it consistent and lowercase with hyphens; predictability is the whole point.

mcqs.explain: Plural noun + HTTP method; no verbs in the path.

mcqs.q: The 'verb' in REST is expressed by:
mcqs.explain: GET/POST/PUT/DELETE carry the action.
Plural nouns keep collections/items consistent.

u:webdev-api-2-idempotency-which-methods.title: Idempotency — which methods and why
u:webdev-api-2-idempotency-which-methods.summary: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is not.

blocks.text: An operation is **idempotent** if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. **GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD** are idempotent; **POST is not** (it typically creates a new resource each call). This matters for safe retries.
Idempotency keys let you make POST safely retryable when a response is lost.

mcqs.explain: POST usually creates a new resource each time.

options: Has the same effect as once
mcqs.explain: Repeats don't change the outcome beyond the first.
Clients can retry idempotent calls without side effects.

u:webdev-api-3-status-code-selection.title: Status code selection
u:webdev-api-3-status-code-selection.summary: Return the code that matches the outcome; don't 200-everything.

items: **201** for created, **200** for OK, **204** for success with no body.
**400** bad input, **401** unauthenticated, **403** forbidden, **404** not found, **409** conflict.
**422** for validation errors (semantically invalid but well-formed).

blocks.text: Returning 200 with an `{error}` body hides failures from clients, proxies, and monitoring. Use the real code.

mcqs.q: A validation failure is best returned as:
mcqs.explain: Client input errors use 4xx (400/422).
Correct status codes convey outcomes.

mcqs.q: A duplicate that conflicts with existing state suits:
mcqs.explain: 409 signals a state conflict.

u:webdev-api-4-pagination-filtering-sort.title: Pagination, filtering, sorting
u:webdev-api-4-pagination-filtering-sort.summary: Return large collections in pages with query params for filter/sort.

blocks.text: Never return unbounded lists. Support **pagination** (offset/limit or cursor), **filtering** (`?status=active`), and **sorting** (`?sort=-createdAt`) via query params. **Cursor** pagination is more stable than offset for large, changing data.
Include total counts / next-cursor in the response so clients can build UIs.

mcqs.q: A safer pagination scheme for large, changing data is:
mcqs.explain: Cursors avoid skipped/duplicated rows as data changes.
?filter=…&sort=… are query params.
Always bound collection responses.

u:webdev-api-5-versioning-strategies.title: Versioning strategies
u:webdev-api-5-versioning-strategies.summary: Version the API so changes don't break existing clients.

items: **URL versioning**: `/v1/users` — simplest and most visible.
**Header versioning**: `Accept: application/vnd.app.v1+json`.
Add fields backward-compatibly; bump the version only for breaking changes.

blocks.text: Breaking changes (removing/renaming fields, changing types) need a new version; additive changes don't.

mcqs.q: The simplest, most visible versioning is:
mcqs.explain: /v1 in the path is explicit and common.
Additive changes don't break existing clients.

mcqs.q: You bump the API version for:
mcqs.explain: Only breaking changes warrant a version bump.

u:webdev-api-6-rate-limiting.title: Rate limiting
u:webdev-api-6-rate-limiting.summary: Cap requests per client to protect the service and ensure fairness.

blocks.text: **Rate limiting** restricts how many requests a client can make in a window (e.g. 100/min) to prevent abuse and overload. Exceeding it returns **429 Too Many Requests**, often with a `Retry-After` header. Common algorithms: token bucket, sliding window.
Key limits by API key or user id, not just IP, so shared IPs (offices, NAT) aren't unfairly blocked.

mcqs.explain: 429 signals the client is being throttled.
It caps request volume per client.
User/key-based limits avoid punishing shared IPs.

u:webdev-api-7-rest-vs-graphql-vs-grpc.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC
u:webdev-api-7-rest-vs-graphql-vs-grpc.summary: REST is resource/HTTP; GraphQL is a query language; gRPC is fast binary RPC.

rows: Simple, cacheable resource APIs over HTTP
Clients that need flexible, exact-shape queries (avoids over/under-fetching)

blocks.text: GraphQL solves over-fetching but complicates caching; gRPC is great internally but not browser-native.

options: Clients fetch exactly the fields they need
mcqs.explain: It avoids over/under-fetching via precise queries.
gRPC is binary Protobuf on HTTP/2.
REST leverages HTTP caching well.

u:webdev-api-8-api-documentation.title: API documentation
u:webdev-api-8-api-documentation.summary: Document endpoints, params, and responses — OpenAPI/Swagger is the standard.

blocks.text: Good APIs are documented so clients can integrate without reading source. **OpenAPI (Swagger)** is the standard machine-readable spec; it can generate interactive docs, client SDKs, and mock servers.
Keep docs in sync by generating them from code/annotations, not writing them by hand separately.

mcqs.q: The standard API spec format is:
mcqs.explain: OpenAPI is the machine-readable industry standard.
Tooling produces docs, SDKs, and mocks from the spec.
Code-generated docs avoid drift.

u:webdev-auth-0-session-based-auth.title: Session-based auth
u:webdev-auth-0-session-based-auth.summary: The server stores a session; the client holds a session id in a cookie.

blocks.text: In **session auth**, on login the server creates a **session** (stored server-side or in a store like Redis) and sends the client a **session id** in a cookie. Each request sends the cookie; the server looks up the session. Logout deletes the session.
Sessions are stateful (server must store them) but easy to revoke — just delete the session.

mcqs.q: In session auth, the client stores:
mcqs.explain: The cookie holds an opaque session id.
The server keeps session state.
Revoking is as simple as removing the session.

u:webdev-auth-1-jwt-structure-signing-ex.title: JWT: structure, signing, expiry
u:webdev-auth-1-jwt-structure-signing-ex.summary: A JWT is header.payload.signature; the signature proves it wasn't tampered with.

blocks.text: A **JWT** has three base64url parts: **header** (algorithm), **payload** (claims like `sub`, `exp`), and **signature**. The server **signs** it with a secret/key; anyone can read the payload, but only the holder of the key can forge a valid signature.
A JWT payload is NOT encrypted — it's just encoded. Never put secrets in it. Always verify the signature and check `exp`.

mcqs.explain: JWTs are header.payload.signature.
Anyone can decode the payload; don't store secrets.
Signature verification detects tampering.

u:webdev-auth-2-access-token-vs-refresh-.title: Access token vs refresh token
u:webdev-auth-2-access-token-vs-refresh-.summary: Short-lived access tokens authorize requests; long-lived refresh tokens mint new ones.

blocks.text: An **access token** is short-lived (minutes) and sent with each request. A **refresh token** is long-lived, stored securely, and used only to obtain a new access token when it expires — limiting the damage if an access token leaks.
Keep access tokens short and refresh tokens well-protected (HttpOnly cookie / secure storage); rotate refresh tokens on use.

mcqs.explain: Short lifetimes limit leak impact.

mcqs.q: A refresh token is used to:
mcqs.explain: It mints fresh access tokens after expiry.

options: The damage from a leaked token
mcqs.explain: A stolen token expires quickly.

u:webdev-auth-3-where-to-store-tokens-an.title: Where to store tokens (and the XSS/CSRF trade-off)
u:webdev-auth-3-where-to-store-tokens-an.summary: localStorage risks XSS; cookies risk CSRF — mitigate whichever you choose.

blocks.text: Storing tokens in **localStorage** exposes them to **XSS** (any injected script can read them). Storing them in **cookies** protects from XSS if `HttpOnly`, but exposes you to **CSRF** (the browser auto-sends cookies).
Common safe pattern: refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; short access token in memory. Add CSRF protection for cookie auth.

mcqs.q: Tokens in localStorage are vulnerable to:
mcqs.explain: Any script can read localStorage (XSS risk).

mcqs.q: HttpOnly cookies help against XSS but expose:
mcqs.explain: Auto-sent cookies enable CSRF without protection.

mcqs.q: A safe pattern stores the refresh token in:
mcqs.explain: HttpOnly Secure cookies resist XSS token theft.

u:webdev-auth-4-oauth-2-0-flow.title: OAuth 2.0 flow
u:webdev-auth-4-oauth-2-0-flow.summary: Delegate access via an authorization server; the app gets tokens, not the password.

blocks.text: **OAuth 2.0** lets a user grant an app limited access to their account on another service **without sharing the password**. The **authorization code** flow: app redirects to the provider → user consents → provider returns a code → app exchanges the code (server-side) for tokens.
Use PKCE for public clients (SPAs/mobile) to protect the code exchange.

mcqs.q: OAuth 2.0 lets an app access an account:
mcqs.explain: It delegates access with tokens, not credentials.

mcqs.q: In the auth-code flow, the code is exchanged for tokens:
options: By the browser directly with the secret
mcqs.explain: The confidential exchange happens server-side (or with PKCE).
PKCE secures the code exchange for public clients.

u:webdev-auth-5-password-hashing-bcrypt-.title: Password hashing: bcrypt, salting
u:webdev-auth-5-password-hashing-bcrypt-.summary: Never store plaintext; hash with a slow, salted algorithm like bcrypt.

blocks.text: Passwords must be stored as **salted hashes**, never plaintext or fast hashes (MD5/SHA). **bcrypt** (or argon2/scrypt) is deliberately **slow** and salts each password, so identical passwords hash differently and brute force is expensive.
A **salt** is a random per-password value that defeats precomputed rainbow tables. bcrypt stores the salt inside the hash string.

mcqs.explain: Use a slow, salted hash like bcrypt/argon2.

options: Defeat rainbow tables / make hashes unique
mcqs.explain: Per-password salts stop precomputed attacks.
A slow hash raises the cost of guessing attacks.

u:webdev-auth-6-https-and-why.title: HTTPS and why
u:webdev-auth-6-https-and-why.summary: HTTPS encrypts traffic with TLS, preventing eavesdropping and tampering.

blocks.text: **HTTPS** wraps HTTP in **TLS**, encrypting data in transit so it can't be read or modified by network intermediaries, and authenticating the server via a certificate. It's mandatory for auth, and required by many browser features (service workers, geolocation).
HTTPS protects data *in transit*; it does not protect data at rest or against XSS/injection.

options: Encryption + integrity + server authentication in transit
mcqs.explain: TLS secures data on the wire and authenticates the server.
App-layer flaws still need their own defenses.

mcqs.q: HTTPS is required for features like:
mcqs.explain: Browsers gate powerful APIs behind secure contexts.

u:webdev-auth-7-xss.title: XSS
u:webdev-auth-7-xss.summary: Cross-site scripting injects malicious scripts; escape output and use CSP.

blocks.text: **XSS** (cross-site scripting) happens when untrusted input is rendered as executable script in a page, letting an attacker run JS in the victim's session. Defend by **escaping/encoding output**, avoiding `innerHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with untrusted data, and setting a **Content-Security-Policy**.
React escapes text by default — the danger returns when you inject raw HTML.

options: Run JavaScript in the victim's page
mcqs.explain: Injected scripts execute in the user's session.
Encoding untrusted output prevents script execution.

mcqs.q: Which reintroduces XSS risk in React?
mcqs.explain: Raw HTML injection bypasses React's escaping.

u:webdev-auth-8-csrf.title: CSRF
u:webdev-auth-8-csrf.summary: Cross-site request forgery abuses auto-sent cookies; defend with tokens/SameSite.

blocks.text: **CSRF** tricks a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted state-changing request to a site where they're authenticated (because the browser auto-sends cookies). Defend with **anti-CSRF tokens**, the **SameSite** cookie attribute, and by requiring a custom header.
CSRF targets cookie-based auth; token-in-header auth (Authorization) is largely immune because the browser won't add it automatically.

mcqs.q: CSRF exploits the fact that browsers:
mcqs.explain: Cookies ride along on cross-site requests.
SameSite and CSRF tokens block forged requests.
Header-token auth isn't auto-sent, so it's largely immune.

u:webdev-auth-9-sql-injection.title: SQL injection
u:webdev-auth-9-sql-injection.summary: Untrusted input in SQL lets attackers alter queries; use parameterized queries.

blocks.text: **SQL injection** occurs when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers change the query (read/delete data, bypass auth). The fix is **parameterized queries / prepared statements** (or an ORM) so input is treated as data, never code.

// BAD:  `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`
// GOOD: db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email])

mcqs.q: The primary defense against SQL injection is:
mcqs.explain: Parameters keep input as data, not SQL.
String-built queries let input become code.
ORMs bind parameters, avoiding injection.

u:webdev-auth-10-helmet-csp-security-hea.title: Helmet, CSP, security headers
u:webdev-auth-10-helmet-csp-security-hea.summary: Security headers harden responses; Helmet sets sensible defaults in Express.

items: **Content-Security-Policy** restricts what scripts/styles/sources can load — a strong XSS mitigation.
**Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)** forces HTTPS.
**X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff**, **X-Frame-Options** (anti-clickjacking).
In Express, **helmet()** sets many of these safely by default.

blocks.text: A tight CSP is one of the most effective defenses against XSS in production.

mcqs.q: A strong header-based XSS mitigation is:
mcqs.explain: CSP restricts allowed script sources.
Helmet applies a suite of security headers.
Strict-Transport-Security enforces HTTPS.

u:webdev-db-0-sql-vs-nosql-choosing-for-.title: SQL vs NoSQL: choosing for a real feature
u:webdev-db-0-sql-vs-nosql-choosing-for-.summary: SQL for structured, relational, transactional data; NoSQL for flexible, high-scale documents.

blocks.text: **SQL** (Postgres/MySQL) enforces a **schema**, relations, and strong **transactions** — ideal when data is structured and consistency matters (payments, orders). **NoSQL** (MongoDB) offers flexible schemas and easy horizontal scale — good for varied documents and high write volume.
Choose by the data and access patterns, not hype. Many apps use both (polyglot persistence).

mcqs.q: Strong multi-row transactions are a strength of:
mcqs.explain: Relational DBs offer robust ACID transactions.

mcqs.q: A flexible, schema-light document store is:
mcqs.explain: MongoDB stores flexible JSON-like documents.

mcqs.q: You should choose a database by:
mcqs.explain: Fit the store to how you read/write the data.

u:webdev-db-1-schema-design-for-your-pro.title: Schema design for your project
u:webdev-db-1-schema-design-for-your-pro.summary: Model entities and relationships; normalize to avoid duplication, denormalize for read speed.

blocks.text: Design the schema around your **entities** and how you **query** them. **Normalization** removes duplication (one source of truth) but needs joins; **denormalization** duplicates data for faster reads. Pick per access pattern.
Start normalized; denormalize deliberately where reads are hot and writes are rare.

mcqs.explain: It keeps one source of truth, avoiding duplicates.
Duplicated data speeds reads but complicates writes.
Model for how the app reads and writes.

u:webdev-db-2-mongodb-documents-and-embe.title: MongoDB documents and embedding vs referencing
u:webdev-db-2-mongodb-documents-and-embe.summary: Embed related data you read together; reference when it's large or shared.

blocks.text: In MongoDB, **embed** sub-documents you almost always read with the parent (e.g. order line items) for one-query reads. **Reference** (store an id) when the related data is large, grows unbounded, or is shared across parents.
Embedding favors read performance and atomic updates; referencing favors normalization and avoids huge documents.

mcqs.q: You should embed data that is:
mcqs.explain: Embed tightly-coupled, co-read data.

mcqs.q: Referencing is better when related data is:
mcqs.explain: References avoid bloated, duplicated documents.
One document = one read, and atomic updates.

u:webdev-db-3-mongoose-schemas-and-valid.title: Mongoose schemas and validation
u:webdev-db-3-mongoose-schemas-and-valid.summary: Mongoose adds schemas, types, and validation on top of MongoDB.

blocks.text: **Mongoose** is an ODM that layers **schemas** (types, required fields, defaults, validators) over MongoDB's schemaless collections, plus middleware/hooks and query helpers. It validates documents before they're saved.
Schema validation catches bad data early, but still validate at the API boundary too.

mcqs.explain: It's an ODM adding structure and validation.
Validation happens on save/validate.
It maps objects to MongoDB documents.

u:webdev-db-4-indexing-for-your-actual-q.title: Indexing for your actual queries
u:webdev-db-4-indexing-for-your-actual-q.summary: Indexes speed reads on queried fields but slow writes and use space.

blocks.text: An **index** is a sorted structure that lets the database find rows without a full scan. Index the fields you **filter/sort by**. Indexes cost extra storage and slow writes, so index for real query patterns, not everything.
A compound index's field order matters — it serves queries that use a leading prefix of its columns.

options: Reads that filter/sort on the field
mcqs.explain: Indexes accelerate lookups on indexed fields.
Each index must be maintained on writes.

mcqs.q: In a compound index, the ___ matters:
mcqs.explain: Queries must use a leading prefix of the index.

u:webdev-db-5-n-plus-1-query-problem.title: N+1 query problem
u:webdev-db-5-n-plus-1-query-problem.summary: Fetching related data in a loop fires one query per item; batch or join instead.

blocks.text: The **N+1 problem**: you run 1 query to get N parents, then 1 query per parent to fetch their children — N+1 total. Fix it by **joining**, using `IN (...)` to batch, or eager-loading (`populate`/`include`).
N+1 is a top hidden performance killer — invisible on small data, crippling at scale.

options: One query per item in a loop plus the initial query
mcqs.explain: It fires N child queries after 1 parent query.
Batch or join to collapse the extra queries.
Query count grows linearly with rows.

u:webdev-db-6-transactions-in-applicatio.title: Transactions in application code
u:webdev-db-6-transactions-in-applicatio.summary: Group operations so they all succeed or all roll back (ACID).

blocks.text: A **transaction** groups multiple operations into one atomic unit: they all commit or all **roll back** on error, keeping data consistent (the A in ACID). Use them for multi-step changes like transferring money between accounts.
Keep transactions short — long ones hold locks and hurt concurrency.

mcqs.explain: Atomicity: commit all or roll back all.

mcqs.q: A classic transaction use case is:
mcqs.explain: Multi-step consistency needs a transaction.
Held locks block other work.

u:webdev-db-7-connection-pooling.title: Connection pooling
u:webdev-db-7-connection-pooling.summary: Reuse a pool of DB connections instead of opening one per request.

blocks.text: Opening a database connection is expensive. A **connection pool** keeps a set of reusable connections; requests borrow and return them. This bounds concurrency and avoids the overhead (and connection-limit exhaustion) of per-request connects.
Size the pool to your DB's connection limit and expected concurrency — too big overwhelms the DB.

mcqs.explain: Pooling amortizes connection setup cost.

mcqs.q: Without pooling, opening a connection per request:
options: Is slow and can exhaust DB limits
mcqs.explain: Per-request connects are costly and hit limits.
Right-size to avoid overwhelming the DB.

u:webdev-db-8-migrations.title: Migrations
u:webdev-db-8-migrations.summary: Migrations version schema changes so every environment stays in sync.

blocks.text: A **migration** is a versioned, repeatable script that evolves the database schema (add a column, create an index). Running migrations in order brings any environment (dev, staging, prod) to the same schema — and they can be rolled back.
Never hand-edit production schemas; commit migrations so changes are reviewable and reproducible.

mcqs.explain: Migrations evolve schema in tracked, ordered steps.

options: In sync with the same schema
mcqs.explain: Everyone applies the same ordered changes.

mcqs.q: You should change production schema by:
mcqs.explain: Migrations make changes reviewable and repeatable.

u:webdev-git-0-branching-strategies.title: Branching strategies
u:webdev-git-0-branching-strategies.summary: Feature branches isolate work; strategies like trunk-based or Git Flow structure merges.

blocks.text: Work on **feature branches** off a main line, then merge via review. **Trunk-based** development keeps short-lived branches merged frequently into main; **Git Flow** uses longer-lived develop/release/hotfix branches. Small, frequent merges reduce conflicts.
Short-lived branches + CI catch problems early; long-lived branches drift and cause painful merges.

options: Isolate work until it's ready to merge
mcqs.explain: They isolate changes for review before merge.
Frequent small merges reduce integration pain.
Divergence makes eventual merges painful.

u:webdev-git-1-merge-vs-rebase.title: Merge vs rebase
u:webdev-git-1-merge-vs-rebase.summary: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase rewrites for a linear history.

blocks.text: **Merge** joins branches with a **merge commit**, preserving the true history. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch for a **linear** history, but rewrites commit hashes.
Never rebase commits that others have already pulled — rewriting shared history breaks their branches.

mcqs.explain: Rebase replays commits for a straight line.
Rewriting shared history breaks collaborators.
Merge keeps the branch topology with a merge commit.

u:webdev-git-2-resolving-conflicts.title: Resolving conflicts
u:webdev-git-2-resolving-conflicts.summary: Conflicts happen when the same lines change on both sides; edit, mark resolved, commit.

blocks.text: A **merge conflict** occurs when two branches change the same lines. Git marks them with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`. You edit the file to the desired result, remove the markers, `git add` it, and complete the merge/rebase.
Pull/rebase often and keep changes small to shrink conflicts; a merge tool helps for big ones.

options: Both branches change the same lines
mcqs.explain: Overlapping edits can't be auto-merged.
Git inserts <<<<<<</=======/>>>>>>> markers.
Stage the resolved file and finish the merge/rebase.

u:webdev-git-3-interactive-rebase-and-sq.title: Interactive rebase and squashing
u:webdev-git-3-interactive-rebase-and-sq.summary: git rebase -i lets you reorder, edit, and squash commits into a clean history.

blocks.text: **Interactive rebase** (`git rebase -i`) lets you **squash**, reword, reorder, or drop commits before sharing — turning messy WIP commits into a clean, reviewable history.
Only clean up commits that haven't been pushed/shared; interactive rebase rewrites history.

mcqs.explain: It rewrites a series of local commits.
Squash merges several commits together.
Avoid rewriting history others rely on.

u:webdev-git-4-gitignore-and-secrets-hyg.title: .gitignore and secrets hygiene
u:webdev-git-4-gitignore-and-secrets-hyg.summary: Never commit secrets or build artifacts; .gitignore keeps them out of the repo.

blocks.text: A **`.gitignore`** lists files Git should not track — `node_modules`, build output, and `.env` secrets. Committing a secret is a leak even if you delete it later, because it stays in history.
If a secret is ever committed, rotate it immediately — removing the file doesn't scrub Git history.

mcqs.explain: Ignore secrets and generated/vendored files.

mcqs.q: If you commit a secret, you should:
mcqs.explain: History retains it; rotate the credential.
It excludes matched paths from version control.

u:webdev-git-5-pull-request-workflow.title: Pull request workflow
u:webdev-git-5-pull-request-workflow.summary: PRs propose changes for review, CI, and discussion before merging.

blocks.text: A **pull request** proposes merging a branch into another, triggering **code review**, automated **CI checks**, and discussion. Keep PRs small and focused so they're easy to review and safe to merge.
A good PR description explains what changed and why, and links the issue — reviewers shouldn't have to guess.

mcqs.explain: PRs gate changes with review and checks.
Small PRs are easier to review and safer.
Context helps reviewers evaluate the change.

u:webdev-git-6-ci-basics.title: CI basics
u:webdev-git-6-ci-basics.summary: Continuous integration runs tests/lint on every push to catch breakage early.

blocks.text: **Continuous Integration (CI)** automatically builds, lints, and tests your code on every push/PR (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI). It catches regressions before merge and enforces quality gates.
Fast, reliable CI is a safety net that lets a team merge frequently with confidence.

mcqs.explain: CI triggers automatically on changes.

u:webdev-git-7-environment-variables-in-.title: Environment variables in production
u:webdev-git-7-environment-variables-in-.summary: Inject config/secrets via the platform's env vars, never bake them into the build.

blocks.text: In production, provide config through the platform's **environment variables / secret manager** (not committed files). Client-side frameworks inline env vars at **build time**, so only put **public** values in client bundles.
A secret placed in a client-side env var (e.g. NEXT_PUBLIC_/VITE_) ships to every browser — never put private keys there.

mcqs.explain: Inject secrets via the platform, not the repo.
Anything in the client bundle is visible to users.
Keep private keys server-side.

u:webdev-git-8-deploying-a-static-site.summary: Build to static files and serve from a CDN host (Netlify, Vercel, Pages).

blocks.text: A **static site** (or SPA build) compiles to HTML/CSS/JS files served from a **CDN** — fast, cheap, and scalable. Hosts like Netlify, Vercel, Cloudflare Pages, and GitHub Pages build on push and deploy globally.
For SPAs, configure a fallback rewrite to index.html so client-side routes don't 404 on refresh.

u:webdev-git-9-deploying-a-node-service.summary: Run the server on a host/PaaS with env vars, a process manager, and health checks.

blocks.text: A **Node service** needs a running process on a host or PaaS (Render, Railway, Fly, a VM, or a container). Set env vars, use a process manager/orchestrator to restart on crash, expose a **health check**, and put it behind HTTPS.

u:webdev-git-10-docker-basics.title: Docker basics
u:webdev-git-10-docker-basics.summary: Containers package the app with its dependencies for consistent runs anywhere.

blocks.text: **Docker** packages your app and all its dependencies into an **image** defined by a `Dockerfile`; a running instance is a **container**. It gives 'runs the same everywhere', eliminating 'works on my machine' drift.
Use small base images and multi-stage builds to keep images lean, and don't bake secrets into the image.
